title: Roberts Shifts Struggling Ohtani to No. 5 for NLDS Game 3, Sparking Lineup Debate
body:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts reshuffled his lineup for Game 3 of the National League Division Series, slipping designated‑hitter Shohei Ohtan​i down to the fifth spot in the batting order – the lowest position he has occupied all season. The move, announced just before the Dodgers took the field in Atlanta, signals Roberts’ willingness to tinker with one of baseball’s most dynamic weapons in an effort to spark a stalled offense against a resilient Atlanta Braves squad.

The decision comes after the Dodgers’ first two games of the series have been a study in contrast. In Game 1, Los Angeles jumped out to a 5‑2 lead, buoyed by Ohtani’s early‑inning homer and a string of timely hits from the middle of the order. The Braves, however, rallied in the later innings and forced extra innings, ultimately falling 9‑5. Game 2 saw the Dodgers’ bats go cold; they managed only two runs on a single run‑scoring double by Mookie Betts, while Atlanta’s pitching staff held firm, handing the Dodgers a 3‑1 defeat that gave the Braves a 2‑0 series lead. With the series now hanging in the balance, Roberts opted to rearrange the lineup in a bid to create more favorable matchups and protect Ohtani from the Braves’ left‑handed relievers who have been effective all postseason.

By moving Ohtani to the number‑five slot, Roberts hopes to give the Japanese star a clearer path to the middle of the order, where he can drive in runs rather than set the table. The adjustment also places right‑handed power hitters—Betts and Freddie Freeman—directly ahead of him, potentially allowing Ohtani to capitalize on any runners he drives in. Moreover, the shift could shield Ohtani from the Braves’ left‑handed specialist, lefty reliever A.J. Minter, who has been dominant against left‑handed hitters in the series. Instead, Ohtani will now face right‑handed pitchers more frequently early in the game, a scenario that aligns better with his career splits.

Roberts’ lineup tweak is not without risk. Ohtani has spent the majority of the 2024 season batting third, a spot that maximized his on‑base opportunities and allowed him to set the tone for the Dodgers’ offense. Dropping him to fifth could diminish his impact if the top of the order fails to get on base, reducing the number of runners he can drive home. Additionally, the move may disrupt the rhythm of other players accustomed to a set order, especially Betts, who has thrived hitting second and could feel the pressure of a new slot. Yet the Dodgers’ bench depth gives Roberts flexibility; veteran outfielder Will Smith and utility man Chris Taylor are poised to fill any gaps, and the club’s bullpen remains one of the strongest in the league, ready to protect leads.

The strategic gamble underscores a broader theme of the postseason: managers must balance statistical optimality with the intangible momentum that star players bring. Roberts, who guided the Dodgers to a World Series title two years ago, has a track record of bold decisions—most notably his use of an eight‑man rotation in the 2022 playoffs. In Atlanta, he appears to be betting that a fresh look at the lineup will jolt a stagnant offense and force the Braves to adjust their pitching strategy. If Ohtani can deliver a clutch hit or two from the fifth spot, the move could be hailed as a masterstroke; if not, critics may argue that the Dodgers’ reliance on tactical shifts has come at the expense of their most potent weapon.

As the series shifts to a decisive Game 3, the Dodgers must find a way to generate runs against a Braves rotation that has been both efficient and adaptable. Roberts’ lineup shuffle is a clear signal that Los Angeles is willing to experiment, even with its marquee talent, to keep the series alive. The next 90 minutes will reveal whether the gamble pays off, setting the tone for the remainder of the NLDS and possibly reshaping how managers deploy elite two‑way players in high‑stakes postseason baseball.
